childNodes.textContent: In any such mixture where there is overlapping, it will be obvious that every one of these mixtures is lighter than any of the mixture parents.
Your screen is three kinds of light, red, green and blue. Drag them over each other. Where two overlap you get a lighter colour, and where all three meet you get white.

Inks work the other way. Each one takes some light away from the white paper, so every overlap is darker than either ink. All three together come close to black.

childNodes.textContent: Additive and subtractive mixtures should be made in appropriate studies in transparence illusions.

Albers asks for these mixtures as illusions, with opaque papers: one thin colour mixing with white or black, and then the first study reversed. Set the square where the colour crosses the grey. To read as light, it has to be lighter than both parents. To read as paint, darker than both. Make one, then the other.
